opus-5.5.text:
I think hallucination is less a bug to be patched and more a natural property of how these models work. A large language model is essentially learning a probability distribution over text. When you ask it something, it generates what is *plausible*, not necessarily what is *true*. Most of the time those two overlap, which is why the models feel so capable. But when they diverge, especially on long-tail facts the model has seen rarely or never, it fills the gap with something that sounds right. In a way, that's the same mechanism that makes it creative.

So I don't expect the model itself to fully "solve" hallucination in the near term. What I see working in practice is a systems approach. First, retrieval: ground the model in real documents, databases, or search results, so it's summarizing and reasoning over evidence rather than recalling from memory. Second, verification: use tools, code execution, or a second pass to check claims, much like how engineers write tests. Third, product design: show sources, express uncertainty, and keep a human in the loop where the stakes are high.

Coming from the infrastructure side, I'd also say a lot of this is an engineering problem as much as a research problem. Enterprises don't need a model that knows everything. They need one that reliably uses *their* data and says "I don't know" when it should. That's achievable today with good pipelines, evaluation, and monitoring.

Longer term, research on calibration, on models knowing what they don't know, will matter a lot. But I'm fairly pragmatic. We didn't wait for perfectly reliable hardware to build reliable computers. We built redundancy and error correction around imperfect components. I think AI will follow a similar path.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say about hallucination is that it's not a bug you can patch in the usual sense. It comes from how these models work. A large language model is, at its core, a system that predicts the next token based on patterns it has seen. It's extremely good at producing something that sounds plausible, and most of the time plausible and correct line up. But the model has no built-in notion of "I don't actually know this." So when it hits a gap, it does exactly what it was trained to do, which is to keep producing fluent text. That fluency is the whole problem. A wrong answer that reads confidently is much harder to catch than a wrong answer that looks obviously broken.

So I don't think of it as "solving" hallucination the way you'd fix a memory leak. I think of it as an engineering problem with a few layers.

The first layer is the model itself. Better training data, better alignment, teaching the model to express uncertainty rather than fill the gap. That helps, and the models have gotten noticeably better. But I'm skeptical you ever drive it to zero at this layer, because you're fighting the basic nature of a probabilistic generator.

The second layer, and honestly the one I find more practical, is grounding. If you want the model to answer questions about your company's documents, don't rely on what it memorized during pretraining. Retrieve the relevant material at inference time and have the model reason over that. This is what people call RAG, and the reason it took off so fast is that it moves the problem from "does the model know this" to "did we fetch the right document," which is a much more familiar engineering question. You can measure it, you can debug it, you can improve it.

The third layer is the system around the model. Verification steps, tool use, having the model call a calculator or a database instead of guessing at numbers, cross-checking outputs. In a real product the model is one component in a pipeline, and a lot of the reliability comes from the pipeline, not from the model alone.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that the right tolerance for hallucination depends entirely on the application. If you're brainstorming marketing copy, a little creativity is a feature. If you're generating a medical summary or a financial report, it's unacceptable. So part of the challenge is not technical at all. It's about being honest with ourselves about where these systems are good enough today and designing the human-in-the-loop accordingly.

Coming from the infrastructure side, this is actually what makes the current moment interesting to me. The frontier isn't just bigger models. It's building the surrounding systems that make a probabilistic component behave reliably enough to be trusted in production. That's where a lot of the real work is.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by “solving” hallucination. A model can produce a very fluent answer without having enough information to support it. Improving the model helps, but fluency itself is not a guarantee of correctness.

From an engineering perspective, I would separate improving the model from making the whole application reliable. If you’re asking a question about a company’s documents, for example, you want the system to retrieve the relevant material and ground its answer in that material. If you need a calculation, you want it to use a calculator. And when there isn’t enough evidence, the system needs to be able to say, “I don’t know.” Of course, retrieval and tools can also fail, so you still need verification.

The tolerance for mistakes also depends on the application. In brainstorming, an unexpected answer might be useful. In a financial or medical workflow, an unsupported answer can be a serious problem. So I wouldn’t treat hallucination as one problem with one universal fix. The practical question is: for this particular task, how do we measure errors, reduce them, and make sure a person can catch the ones that remain?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish between generating something plausible and knowing that it’s true. A language model is trained to predict language, so a fluent answer doesn’t necessarily mean it has reliable evidence behind it.

That makes hallucination more than a model-training problem. You can improve the model, but you also need to build a system around it: give it access to relevant information, let it use tools to check facts, and teach it to say, “I don’t have enough information,” instead of always producing an answer. Even then, retrieving a document doesn’t guarantee the model will interpret it correctly.

The level of reliability you need also depends on the application. If you’re brainstorming, an unexpected answer can be useful. If you’re making a medical or financial decision, the same behavior can be unacceptable. So I would frame the challenge as reducing errors, making them easier to detect, and limiting their consequences. I wouldn’t assume that simply making the model larger will solve all three.
